en.stage1Journal: Nearest 10: When we round to the nearest 10, we look at the ones digit. If it is 0 to 4, we round down to the lower multiple of 10. If it is 5 to 9, we round up to the next multiple of 10.
en.stage1Task1: Examine the items on the work benches
en.stage1Task2: Choose something made of matter that will dissolve in water
en.stage1Task3: Inflate the balloon with the button
en.stage1Text2: Today we are going to perform experiments to determine what makes up matter
en.stage1Text3: Let's move into the next room. You can move around with the WASD keys or the arrow keys.
en.stage1Text4: Here we are in the lab! Let’s investigate matter.
en.stage1Text5: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. The amount of space it takes up is called its volume.
en.stage1Text6: All the substances around us are made of matter, even the air we breathe!
en.stage1Text7: There are 5 items on the workbenches. Let’s examine each one and discover which are matter. Walk up to a bench to take a closer look.
en.stage1Text8: On this table is a patch of light from a lamp. Select it to take a closer look or click the cross to leave the table.
en.stage1Text9: This lamp produces light. When light hits the table, some of it reflects off the surface and reaches your eyes, allowing you to see it.
en.stage1Text10: Select all correct statements about the mass and volume of this sample.
en.stage1Text11: On this table are a ceramic cup filled with water and a pile of sugar cubes. Click either item to learn about its properties. Click the cross to leave the table.
en.stage1Text12: This ceramic cup of water shows two states of matter. The ceramic cup is a solid, and the water inside is a liquid. Both have mass and take up space. The cup keeps its shape, while the water takes the shape of its container without changing volume.
en.stage1Text13: Sugar cubes are solids with mass and volume. When a cube dissolves, its tiny sugar particles spread through the water. The sugar is still there, but its particles are too small to see. This is a great example of matter that can be divided into tiny particles that are too small to be seen.
en.stage1Text14: On this table is a balloon filled with air. Beside it, you’ll see a shadow cast by a cube. Click the balloon or the shadow to explore its properties. Click the cross to leave the table.
en.stage1Text15: The stretchy rubber is a solid, and the air inside is a mixture of gases. Both have mass and take up space. The air spreads out to fill the balloon, and adding more air stretches the rubber.
en.stage1Text16: This is the shadow cast by the cube. The cube blocks some of the light from the light source, so less light reaches this part of the table. The shadow shows where the light is blocked. The cube has mass and takes up space, but the shadow itself has no mass.
en.stage1Text23: Oh look, a tank of water has appeared inside the lab. Let's go look at it.
